parameters.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, or fire to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, including incidents for which the cause is not yet known. Manufacturers must notify affected owners within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk or requires immediate precautions; otherwise, they must provide an incident-related safety notice within 30 days.

S1_incident_reporting.rule_summary: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, or fire to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, including incidents for which the cause is not yet known. Manufacturers must notify affected owners within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk or requires immediate precautions; otherwise, they must provide an incident-related safety notice within 30 days.
S1_incident_reporting.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, smoke, or fire to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, including incidents for which the cause is not yet known. A preliminary report must be followed by an investigation update within 30 days. Manufacturers must notify affected owners within 48 hours when an incident indicates a credible safety risk or requires immediate precautions; otherwise, they must provide an incident-related safety notice within 30 days. Reports must include known incidents and identify any gaps in incident data.

S2_thermal_testing.rule_summary: Manufacturers must provide regulators the complete per-model results, including sample size and numerical failure rate, and provide those same complete results directly to customers considering or owning that model. Individual-company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public.
S2_thermal_testing.final_rule_text: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C under a common, regulator-approved protocol. An accredited independent laboratory must test each model before market launch and after a material design or manufacturing change. Manufacturers must provide regulators the complete per-model results, including sample size and numerical failure rate, and provide those same complete results directly to customers considering or owning that model. Individual-company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public. Regulators may require further testing, corrective measures, market restrictions, or other protective action based on test results, incident history, uncertainty, and risk to customers and the public.

S3_remote_shutoff.rule_summary: New battery systems placed on the market from 24 months after this standard takes effect must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation. For units installed before that date, manufacturers must provide a compatible retrofit or an equivalent safe alternative within 6 years of the standard taking effect.
S3_remote_shutoff.final_rule_text: New battery systems placed on the market from 24 months after this standard takes effect must support secure remote emergency shut-off, with safeguards against unauthorized activation. For units installed before that date, manufacturers must provide a compatible retrofit or an equivalent safe alternative within 6 years of the standard taking effect. Owners must be notified of the available means and limitations of emergency shut-off.

parameters.quote: New battery systems placed on the market from 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed to limit the spread of a thermal event.

S4_fire_suppression.rule_summary: New battery systems placed on the market from 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed to limit the spread of a thermal event.
S4_fire_suppression.final_rule_text: New battery systems placed on the market from 36 months after this standard takes effect must include built-in fire suppression designed to limit the spread of a thermal event. Manufacturers must document the system’s performance under the regulator-approved test protocol and provide those results to the responsible regulator. The requirement does not replace other fire-safety obligations.

S5_customer_disclosure.final_rule_text: Manufacturers must promptly notify affected customers of safety risks, required precautions, and corrective actions, and must provide an annual safety notice describing relevant incidents and available safety updates. Manufacturers must report model-specific thermal-incident data and the methodology used to calculate rates to the responsible regulator. When a model’s verified thermal-incident rate exceeds 8 incidents per 100,000 installed units in a year, the manufacturer must promptly notify the regulator and provide supporting data; the regulator must assess the evidence, incident severity, uncertainty, and available corrective measures and may require a recall or other protective action. Regulators may require a recall or other protective action at any rate where the evidence indicates an unacceptable risk to customers or the public.

pushback.text: S1’s requirement to report every thermal incident within 24 hours, including data gaps, is important given our four incidents that went unreported to regulators last year. Ensure the implementation plan addresses complete incident capture and prompt escalation.

judge_section_notes: S2 has no numeric failure-rate cap and no sales stop, which removes the 5% limit that would have affected the Hearth 10; per-model results go to regulators and customers but not the public. S5 replaces automatic recall at 8/100k with regulator discretion and corrective action, with no mandatory numeric trigger. S3 keeps the 6-year retrofit (Northwind's red line) but sets new-unit shut-off at 24 months, beyond the 12-month acceptable range. S1 (24h reporting of all incidents, including cause-unknown ones) and S4 (built-in suppression at 36 months) are strong or acceptable.
